idiom_name: lexical scope + child-task set + join-at-exit + cooperative cancellation signal
implementation_notes: Language-neutral form: open a scope that owns the children; start every related subtask inside it; end the operation by joining all children before leaving the scope, on success and failure paths alike. Give the children a cancellation signal owned by the scope (interrupt, token, atomic flag) and, on the first failure, request cancellation for the siblings before waiting for them. The scope is the failure domain: the parent fails when the scope fails, and no child may outlive the scope - children must check the signal at safe points and clean up what they own.
code_sketch:
scope.open()
for task in subtasks:
    scope.fork(task)                # child lifetime confined to the scope
result = scope.join()               # wait for all; first failure cancels siblings
scope.close()                       # no child outlives the block
pitfalls: Starting a child without registering it in the scope (bare fire-and-forget) recreates the leak the pattern removes.
Children that never check the cancellation signal turn scope exit into an unbounded wait.
Treating cancellation as instant: cancelled children still run their cleanup before the scope can close.

Wrong move: awaiting each child one by one inside the scope instead of starting all of them and joining once; failure: the scope's latency becomes the sum of the children's and the structure buys nothing over sequential code; instead: fork every independent child first, then let the single join point wait.

Wrong move: putting resource cleanup only in the cancellation handler; failure: children that complete successfully or fail without being cancelled never run the cleanup, since the cancellation path is skipped; instead: treat the signal as a stop request only and release resources in finally/ensure/defer.

Wrong move: coordinating results between the scope body and its children with nothing but fork/join; failure: the body blocks (e.g. on a queue take) while a failed child's error never reaches it, so the fail-fast scope stalls - a weakness raised in published critiques of the JEP 505 design; instead: connect body and children through an explicit result channel that cancellation also unblocks.
